opus-5.5.text:
I think the resistance was very understandable, and honestly I respect it. For many animators, motion isn't just data. It's craft. A good animator spends years learning timing, weight, exaggeration, how a character should "feel" when it lands a jump or turns its head. So when a technical team comes along and says, "We can take a human video and automatically produce the animation," it can sound like we're saying all that skill can be replaced by a camera and an algorithm. That's threatening, and it also feels a bit disrespectful to the art form.

There's also a real aesthetic point. Animation isn't simply a copy of reality. If you look at classic animation, the motion is often deliberately unrealistic: squash and stretch, anticipation, holds. Directly transferring human motion can look stiff or uncanny, like rotoscoping done badly. So when people pushed back, part of what they were saying was, "Realism isn't the goal. Expressiveness is." I think that critique was correct, and it pushed us to think harder.

And then there are practical concerns: data, attribution, jobs. Who owns the motion? Whose performance is being learned from? Will studios use this to cut people? Those aren't irrational fears. Every time a new tool arrives in a creative industry, people ask them, and they should.

My own view is that the right positioning is as a tool, not a replacement. For a lot of creators, especially small teams or independent artists, getting a rough, physically plausible motion quickly is enormously valuable. Then the artist does what humans are good at: deciding what the shot needs, exaggerating, stylizing, giving the character personality. The tedious part gets lighter. The creative part stays with people.

So I see the initial resistance less as opposition and more as a signal. It told us what the community values, and what we had to respect if we wanted the technology to be useful to them. Over time, as people actually tried it and saw it could save them effort without taking away their control, the conversation became much more constructive. But I don't think we should ever dismiss those concerns. Technologists need to listen to the people whose work we're touching.

fable-5.1.text:
I think I understood it, honestly, before we even published anything. When we started working on generating animation from human videos, we were coming at it as researchers who care about motion, about data, about whether a model can learn structure from the real world. The animation community was coming at it from a completely different place. For them, animation is not a byproduct of capturing reality. It's the opposite. It's the deliberate exaggeration, the timing, the squash and stretch, the choices an animator makes precisely because the real world doesn't look like that.

So when they saw a project that said, in effect, "give us a video of a person and we'll turn it into animation," what many of them heard was: "we're going to take the craft out of this." And I don't think that reaction was unreasonable. Rotoscoping has a long and complicated history in that world. Animators have always been a bit wary of anything that traces reality too closely, because the results often look lifeless. There's that uncanny stiffness that everyone recognizes immediately.

There was also, I think, a real anxiety about labor and about where value sits. If a studio can get something passable out of a camera and a model, what happens to the junior animators who learn the craft by doing exactly that kind of in-between work? That's not a technical objection, it's a social one, and we as a research group were not initially very good at hearing it as such. We tended to respond with benchmarks and demos, which is a bit like answering a question about meaning with a spreadsheet.

What changed my own thinking was spending time actually sitting with animators and watching them work. I realized the interesting problem was never "replace the animator." It was: can the system learn the physical plausibility and the rhythm of real human motion as raw material, and then hand control back to the artist to exaggerate, to break the rules on purpose? Once we started framing the work that way, as a tool that gives you a starting point you can push around rather than a finished output, the conversation got much more productive. Some of our harshest early critics ended up being the people who gave us the most useful feedback about what a good motion prior should actually preserve.

So I'd say the resistance was partly a misunderstanding of what we were trying to do, but it was also partly us misunderstanding what animation is. Both sides had to move.

astra-6.text:
I think that resistance is understandable. For animators, movement isn’t just a set of joint positions. It’s timing, expression, and choices about what to exaggerate or leave out. So when you say you’re generating animation from human videos, people may hear, “We’re going to automate your craft,” and wonder whether you understand what their work involves.

The distinction I would make is between capturing motion and creating a performance. A video can provide a starting point, but that doesn’t mean it gives you the performance you want for a particular character. I see the technology as a way to reduce some of the labor involved in getting to that starting point, while giving animators room to shape the result. But we have to demonstrate that in a useful workflow; simply calling it a tool doesn’t resolve people’s concerns.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that resistance is understandable. Animation is much more than reproducing human movement. Animators make choices about timing, exaggeration, and emotion, so saying that we can generate animation from a human video can sound as though we’re reducing their craft to a technical problem—or trying to replace them.

The way I see it, the goal is to give artists a useful starting point. Capturing motion from video can reduce some of the repetitive work, but the animator still needs control over the performance and the style. We have to demonstrate that value in their workflow, and take their concerns seriously.
